seo_title: Can You Sue After Insurance Appraisal? Texas Law Explained
meta_description: Can you sue after insurance appraisal? Learn which Texas claims survive an award, when awards get set aside, and what Ortiz and Barbara Tech mean for you.
h1: Can You Sue After Insurance Appraisal?
primary_keyword: can you sue after insurance appraisal
secondary_keywords: sue insurance company after appraisal Texas
excerpt: An appraisal award usually settles the amount of loss, but some Texas claims survive. Learn what Ortiz and Barbara Technologies mean and when awards can be challenged.
key_takeaways: A paid appraisal award generally ends breach-of-contract claims for more benefits.
Ortiz limits most bad-faith claims after payment unless there is an independent injury.
Barbara Technologies allows Prompt Payment Act claims to survive award payment.
Awards can be set aside for fraud, mistake, or appraisers exceeding authority.
body_html:
You can sometimes sue after insurance appraisal in Texas, but appraisal narrows what is left to sue over. The award generally settles the amount of loss, and paying it typically ends a breach-of-contract claim. Coverage disputes, late-payment claims under the Prompt Payment Act, and challenges to a flawed award may still proceed in court.

Appraisal is designed to resolve one thing: how much the covered damage is worth. It is not designed to resolve every disagreement between a policyholder and an insurer. That gap is why many Texas property owners ask whether signing on to appraisal means giving up their right to go to court.

This article explains what appraisal settles, which claims may survive an award, when courts set awards aside, and how Texas Supreme Court decisions shape the answer. It is general information, not legal advice. If you are considering a lawsuit, talk to a Texas attorney about your specific facts.

What Does Insurance Appraisal Actually Decide?

The appraisal clause in most Texas property policies applies when you and the insurer fail to agree on the amount of loss. Each side appoints an appraiser, the appraisers choose an umpire, and an award signed by any two of the three generally fixes the amount of loss. Learn how the process works in what is an insurance appraisal.

Under State Farm Lloyds v. Johnson (Tex. 2009), appraisers determine the amount of loss and may assess causation as it relates to the extent of damage. They do not decide coverage or liability. Those questions remain for the insurer and, if necessary, the courts.

Texas courts generally favor appraisal because it resolves valuation disputes quickly and inexpensively, using people who understand construction and pricing. That preference is part of why awards are so difficult to overturn once they are signed and paid.

So appraisal answers how much. It does not necessarily answer whether the policy pays, whether the insurer paid on time, or whether the insurer handled the claim fairly.

Coverage Disputes vs Amount-of-Loss Disputes

IssueDecided in appraisal?Can it reach court after appraisal?
Repair cost, scope, pricingYesGenerally no, unless the award is set aside

Can You Sue for Breach of Contract After Appraisal?

Usually not, once the insurer timely pays the award. In Ortiz v. State Farm Lloyds (Tex. 2019), the Texas Supreme Court held that when an insurer pays an appraisal award in accordance with the policy, the policyholder generally cannot pursue a breach-of-contract claim for more policy benefits. The court reasoned that the insurer did what the contract required: it paid the amount of loss determined under the policy's own process.

This is why choosing the right appraiser and building a thorough estimate matter so much. In most cases, the award is the number. Any item your appraiser fails to raise, document, or negotiate during appraisal is very difficult to recover later through a lawsuit.

Can You Sue for Bad Faith After Insurance Appraisal?

Ortiz also held that payment of an appraisal award generally bars common-law and statutory bad-faith claims (such as claims under Insurance Code chapter 541) when the only damages sought are the policy benefits the award already covers. A policyholder may still have a claim if they can show an injury independent of the right to policy benefits, but those cases are uncommon.

Conduct that may raise bad-faith concerns includes:

  • Refusing to pay a claim without a reasonable investigation
  • Misrepresenting policy terms
  • Failing to attempt a prompt, fair settlement once liability is reasonably clear
  • Failing to explain the basis for denying or underpaying a claim

Whether any of these support a lawsuit after appraisal depends heavily on the facts and the damages involved. That is a question for an attorney.

Late Payment Claims Under the Texas Prompt Payment Act

Timing is one area where appraisal does not end the inquiry. In Barbara Technologies v. State Farm Lloyds (Tex. 2019), the Texas Supreme Court held that an insurer's payment of an appraisal award does not, by itself, bar a claim under the Texas Prompt Payment of Claims Act (Insurance Code chapter 542).

The Act generally requires insurers to:

  • Acknowledge a claim within 15 days of notice
  • Accept or reject it within 15 business days after receiving requested information (with an extension of up to 45 days in some cases)
  • Pay within 5 business days after notifying the policyholder that the claim is accepted

If an insurer was liable for the claim and delayed payment beyond those deadlines, statutory interest and attorney's fees may be at issue even after the award is paid. Our Texas claim deadline calculator helps you track these dates, and the statute is available on the Texas Legislature's statutes site.

Tip: Keep a dated record of when you reported the claim, when the insurer requested information, when you provided it, and when each payment arrived. Those dates matter for any prompt-payment analysis.

When Can an Appraisal Award Be Set Aside?

Texas courts give appraisal awards strong deference and indulge every reasonable presumption in their favor. Still, an award can be challenged in limited circumstances.

Fraud, accident, or mistake

An award produced through fraud or collusion, or one reflecting a clear mistake showing the appraisers did not make an honest judgment, may be set aside.

Appraisers exceeding their authority

If appraisers decide coverage questions, value items outside the scope of the claim, or fail to follow the policy's procedure, a court may disregard all or part of the award.

Lack of independence

An appraiser with an undisclosed financial interest in the outcome, such as a contractor who will perform the repairs, can give the other side grounds to challenge the award. See can contractors participate in insurance appraisal.

Can the insurance company sue after appraisal?

Yes, on the same grounds. Insurers sometimes challenge awards they believe were based on fraud, exceeded the appraisers' authority, or included uncovered damage. Insurers may also pay the award while maintaining that some portion is not covered.

What If Hidden Damage Appears After Appraisal?

Sometimes repairs uncover damage nobody could see during appraisal, such as rotted decking under a roof or wet framing behind walls. Whether that damage can be added depends on the award's language, the policy, and whether the new damage was truly outside what the appraisers considered. A carefully worded award that addresses scope helps. Our article on whether appraisal can reopen a closed insurance claim covers related questions, and supplemental insurance claims explained outlines how supplements work.

Common Misunderstandings About Appraisal and Lawsuits

  • "Appraisal ends every possible dispute." It settles the amount of loss. Coverage and prompt-payment issues can remain.
  • "Winning appraisal guarantees full payment." The insurer applies your deductible, prior payments, depreciation, and any coverage positions to the award.
  • "You automatically lose the right to sue." Some claims survive, but the scope is narrower after a paid award.
  • "You can always relitigate the number." Courts rarely disturb awards, so the appraisal itself is your best chance to get the amount right.

Texas Weather Claims and Pre-Suit Notice

For hail, wind, and other weather-related property claims, Texas Insurance Code chapter 542A generally requires a policyholder to give the insurer written notice at least 61 days before filing suit, including the specific amount alleged to be owed. Insurers may also request an inspection or demand appraisal during that period. If you are considering litigation on a Texas storm claim, plan for this timeline and talk to an attorney early. Homeowners in hail-prone areas like Fort Worth and the rest of North Texas encounter this process often.

Next Steps: Get the Appraisal Right the First Time

Because Texas law treats a paid award as largely final on the amount of loss, the appraisal itself is where most of the value is won or lost. Keep complete records, choose an experienced, independent appraiser, document every item of damage, and consult an attorney about any coverage or timing concerns before the award is signed.

Records every policyholder should keep

  • The full policy, declarations page, and endorsements
  • Your first notice of loss and the claim number, with dates
  • Every estimate, revised estimate, and payment letter from the insurer
  • Photos, videos, measurements, and contractor estimates
  • The written appraisal demand, appraiser and umpire appointments, and the signed award
  • Proof of the date each payment was received

Our claim documentation checklist can help you organize these from the start.

When legal review may help

An attorney's review may be worth considering if the insurer denied part of the claim on coverage grounds, paid significantly late, refused to pay the award, reserved rights on items included in the award, or if you believe the opposing appraiser or umpire was not impartial. Attorneys typically review the policy, the claim timeline, correspondence, and the award itself. Your appraiser can work alongside counsel, but on an appraisal assignment the appraiser does not give legal advice or act as your attorney.

faqs.q: Does accepting appraisal waive my right to sue in Texas?
faqs.a: Not entirely. Appraisal generally settles the amount of loss, and a timely paid award usually ends breach-of-contract claims for more policy benefits. However, coverage disputes, Prompt Payment Act claims, and challenges based on fraud or appraisers exceeding their authority may still proceed. This is general information, so consult a Texas attorney about your situation.

faqs.q: Can I get prompt payment interest after an appraisal award?
faqs.a: Possibly. In Barbara Technologies v. State Farm Lloyds (2019), the Texas Supreme Court held that paying an appraisal award does not by itself bar a claim under the Texas Prompt Payment of Claims Act. If the insurer was liable and missed statutory deadlines, interest and attorney's fees may be at issue. An attorney can evaluate your timeline.

faqs.q: Can I challenge an appraisal award I disagree with?
faqs.a: Disagreeing with the number is not enough. Texas courts give awards strong deference and typically set them aside only for fraud, accident, or mistake, for appraisers exceeding their authority, or for serious procedural problems such as an appraiser lacking required independence. That is why preparing a thorough, well-documented case during appraisal is so important.

faqs.q: What happens if the insurer refuses to pay the appraisal award?
faqs.a: If an insurer fails to pay a valid award according to the policy, the policyholder may have a breach-of-contract claim to enforce it, along with potential Prompt Payment Act remedies. Document the date the award was signed and delivered, and consult a Texas attorney if payment does not arrive within the timeframe your policy and Texas law provide.
